Skip next section Iran working to finalize Hormuz agreement with Oman 08/17/2026 August 17, 2026 Iran working to finalize Hormuz agreement with Oman Iran 's Foreign Ministry said Monday that it was working to finalize a joint statement with Oman on a plan to manage the passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz . "An understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route," said foreign affairs spokesman Esmail Baghaei, conceding that talks with Oman had progressed slowly. "We had planned, and still plan, to finalize the understanding in the form of a package: the map plus a joint statement," he told reporters in Tehran . Although Baghaei did not elaborate on the plan, previous details have suggested that ships could be expected to enter the key waterway through a route closer to Iran before exiting on a route closer to Oman. It is not expected that ships would have to pay fees or tolls. The announcement came as a 60-day negotiating period to agree a permanent peace deal between the United States and Iran expired, with no word of an extension and both sides seemingly as far apart as they were two months ago. The US has sought an acceptable deal on reopening the strait before ending its blockade of Iranian ports and it was not immediately clear whether the new Iran-Oman deal would meet Washington's expectations. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ix8u Skip next section Israeli minister calls for more 'targeted killings' in Gaza 08/17/2026 August 17, 2026 Israeli minister calls for more 'targeted killings' in Gaza Monday's meeting between Benjamin Netanyahu and US envoy Jared Kushner comes after Israel 's national security minister called for dozens more Palestinians to be killed "every night" in "targeted killings" in the Gaza Strip . Far-right hardliner Itamar Ben-Gvir made the remarks in a podcast with a former Gaza hostage which went live on Saturday evening. "I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza, removing 30, 40 people every night," he said, specifying that he was not only referring to members of militant groups. "Not just those who pose an immediate threat; there are people there who are not worthy of life. They shouldn't live. They're not even people." Ben-Gvir is the chairman of the "Otzma Yehudit" ("Jewish Power") party and a member of Netanyahu's government, but he said he disagrees with the prime minister's plans for post-war Gaza. Meanwhile, Iran 's deputy foreign minister condemned the comments in a post on social media on Monday morning. "This Zionist criminal speaks at the same time of expelling Palestinians and of settlement construction across the entire Gaza Strip," wrote Kazem Gharibabadi. "These confessions must be recorded and preserved for the day of reckoning and for the trial of these criminals." In the past, similar statements by Ben-Gvir and other Israeli officials have been presented to the UN's world court as evidence of genocidal intent. Israel denies that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide. https://p.dw.com/p/5Iwjq Skip next section Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem 08/17/2026 August 17, 2026 Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hosted US President Donald Trump 's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Jerusalem on Monday as a US-backed plan for the governance of the Gaza Strip remained stalled. The meeting, which comes a day after Kushner met with Hamas leader Khalil ‌Al-Hayya in Cairo, Egypt , was also attended by Trump's Board ‌of ​Peace envoy for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair , according to media reports. Earlier this month, Netanyahu publicly rejected a Trump proposal which would have seen the militant group Hamas disarm and Israeli troops withdraw from the Gaza Strip . Trump had said the agreement would be carried out in phases, with Israeli forces gradually replaced in the devastated Palestinian territory by an "International ​Stabilization Force" which would work alongside a new Palestinian police force. Hamas has said it agreed to the plan but the deal has stalled, with Netanyahu insisting that Israel's military will only withdraw once Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza have been completely disarmed. Israeli troops continue to occupy about 60% of the enclave and Netanyahu has previously threatened to advance further. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/26/iran-.text: Iran and Oman's foreign ministers met in Tehran on Tuesday to discuss a phased approach to managing ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a criticial waterway that remains effectively closed since the war in Iran started in February.Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi "discussed a phased framework that could provide a practical and implementable basis for moving forward," a joint statement said.The proposed framework includes a "joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and a mine-clearing project in the waterway.Further negotiations will establish a "permanent navigational corridor and future administration of the Strait, as well as a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services", the statement added."I am hopeful we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz," Albusaidi wrote on X, adding that the countries will work towards a permanent solution, as well as an agreement on who will administer the strait.Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state television that the temporary route for marine traffic enterting the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman would pass entirely through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass through both Iranian waters and Omani waters.Iran and Oman will hold further talks over 30 to 60 days, Gharibabadi added.The talks come a week after US President Donald Trump threatened to launch strikes against Oman if it "gets in the way" of talks between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz."If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s--- out of them, Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Monday, as June's US-Iran memorandum of understanding expired.It is unclear whether Trump will accept the deal reached between Iran and Oman.Iran's president and other senior officials also discussed the strait with a Pakistani delegations that left Tehran on Tuesday after holding talks aimed at reviving negotiations to end the war in Iran, Pakistan's military said.

Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen More than a third of Britons feel that the Labour government has done a ‘bad job’ on climate issues since taking office in 2024. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Extreme heat Analysis Beyond the heatwave: what it really takes for climate warnings to cut through in the UK Natalie Wint As trust in institutions wavers, experts say local, collective action is more effective in driving change Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Share Wildfires, excess deaths, hosepipe bans, school closures: this summer many British people have experienced the often devastating effects of the climate crisis in ways they had not before. In that sense, policymakers and climate experts have a unique opportunity to engage with the public about what needs to happen to better prepare the country for the years ahead. But as trust in institutions wavers – and yellowed, drought-stricken grass begins to recover – can the messaging cut through? This week, reflecting on a summer as “hot as hell” , the UN’s head of climate, Simon Stiell, said: “Climate is sometimes seen as a partisan issue, as territory in the culture wars. That is palpably false.” He said: “Climate cuts across the core concerns of voters, whatever their politics: [affecting] family health, community safety and economic stability; affordable food and available water; jobs, business costs and household bills.” In policy terms, there are two ways to lessen the impact: climate mitigation and climate adaptation. Mitigation involves reducing the emissions causing global heating, while adaptation is about responding to its impacts. For climate experts and policymakers, the distinction is important. But recent research conducted by Climate Outreach, a charity specialising in climate communication research, found that people in the UK do not generally divide climate action into these two categories. “People talk about them interchangeably,” said Chris Pollard, a senior researcher at Climate Outreach. Only about half of those in the study understood the term “climate adaptation”. However, the mixed response to the government-issued “severe alert” to wildfire risk in mid-August highlighted the need for clearer communication on both. While some recipients of the notification decried the top-down “overreach”, others complained the government should instead be focusing on decarbonising the energy grid. As the impacts of the climate crisis become more immediate, the question is not only whether people understand the difference, but whether their understanding leads to action and support for policies that tackle both. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from wildfires near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA “What people are wanting is: what works, and how they do it,” said Rowena Hill, a professor of resilience, emergencies and disaster science at Nottingham Trent University. But there is a fine line to tread when it comes to responsibility. The recent £75m Let’s Save Water campaign, which advised people to treat water as a precious resource and cut their daily use by 28 litres, prompted questions about whether this put too much responsibility on consumers, given that a huge contributor to water loss is ageing infrastructure and a lack of investment in the water system. “Empowerment is really hindered because of that lack of clear accountability,” Hill said. The “you are responsible” needed to become “we are responsible”, she added. And how do you make sure that people trust the message? Accountability matters, but confidence in political institutions is low, with research suggesting that elected representatives misperceive public support for climate policies . More than a third of Britons surveyed by Ipsos this summer said the Labour government had done a “bad job” dealing with the climate crisis since coming into power in July 2024. Trust also comes from making climate risks relevant to people’s lives. “It is about the community understanding the community’s risks, rather than the community understanding how they might fit into this really big geography of a risk analysis,” Hill said. “The value of our environmental surroundings, how people use that and what that means to the local community is really important.” The response to the felling of the Sycamore Gap tree offers one example: the grief and anger that followed demonstrated people’s strong connection to their immediate environment. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The Sycamore Gap tree in 2008. Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian Climate Outreach uses the seven British segments produced by More in Common to understand how people’s values differ, and where messages can resonate across groups. As Pollock puts it, messaging should focus on “things that cut across values” using framings that “appeal to as many people as possible and do not alienate”. In a time of culture wars, this advice is not just theoretical. Greener Henley, a climate and nature-based action charity, is using it. “We’re appealing to people across the political spectrum,” said Kate Oldridge, the charity’s executive director. The charity used research on the segmentation of the local community to tailor its pledges, inviting people to commit to simple, practical actions that are “very relevant to people’s lives”. Oldbridge said this approach could drive tangible change beyond the community. “It also serves to inspire by demonstrating to policymakers that here’s a community that can do something really amazing,” she said. For example, the charity is working with schools to implement climate action plans recommended by the government, including offering practical help to keep classrooms cool in summer and better defend playgrounds against flooding. For the volunteers, taking part provides a sense of hope and collective purpose. Oldbridge said: “They see that there’s a problem. They want to do something, but it also brings them joy to get out there and do something. It makes them feel more hopeful, more inspired. “We feel massively supported and our anxiety alleviated by the fact that we’re actually doing this work and doing it with each other.” Explore more on these topics Extreme heat Climate crisis Extreme weather Communities Wildfires analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Cross-party talks needed to tackle climate crisis, say Lib Dems ‘We’re not remotely prepared’: Labour MPs fear party has gone soft on climate crisis Three-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave looms Hotter summers may force RHS to move hydrangeas to north of England Parts of England under heat alert with 30C temperatures possible Drought declared in parts of Wales as July on course to be driest in nearly 200 years MPs call on UK government to host televised emergency briefing on climate crisis Western Europe records hottest-ever June as heatwaves intensify Ian McEwan says pessimism ‘a bigger problem than climate change’ Today in Focus The security report the UK government doesn’t want you to see – podcast Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
